extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literature; playwrights and critics studying Aristotelian poetics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for composing or analysing tragedy according to Aristotle as presented in a literary-critical textbook: what tragedy is, its constituent features (action, character, language, form), its emotional aims (pity/fear), and the nature of katharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy is Imitation (mimesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation (μίμησις) — the generic category it shares with all fine arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The work should operate by representing actions and characters rather than simply recounting events; imitation as a principle separates tragic art from non-imitative discourse. Evaluate whether the play enacts and embodies its material (through performance, embodiment, staging) rather than merely narrating it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seriousness (σπουδαία πράξις) — action must be serious and grave
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation of an action that is serious (neither ludicrous nor morally trivial); concerned with a serious end (eudaimonia / true well‑being).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate 'serious' with mere high social rank; seriousness refers to the nature and ethical weight of the action. Avoid comic or trivial subject-matter; the plot should deal with matters of grave human significance. Beware the anti-pattern of equating seriousness solely with aristocratic protagonists (French critics' mistake).

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness (τελεία) — the action must be whole/complete
rubrics_metrics.description: The imitated action must be complete (having a beginning, middle, and end) — a unitary and self-contained action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the plot forms a coherent whole with necessary causal links; avoid episodic or disjointed arrangements that fail to present a single, integrated action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude (μέγεθος) — of a certain magnitude/significance
rubrics_metrics.description: The action must be of a certain magnitude: sufficiently large in significance (and traditionally understood also as having due length or appropriate scope).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magnitude denotes the significance and scale appropriate to tragic treatment (not merely physical length). Evaluate whether events and stakes are weighty enough to sustain tragic treatment; beware misreading magnitude as only duration or literal length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form: action not narrative (dramatic, not epic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is differentiated from Epic by being dramatic (presented in action/performance) rather than narrative (told by a single speaker).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The work should present events through enacted scenes and characters in speech and action rather than extended narration. Judge by how effectively the play uses dramatic means (dialogue, performance) to realise the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and 'several kinds of embellishment'
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition requires 'language embellished with each kind of artistic ornament, the several kinds being found in separate parts of the play' — verse and song, with verse in dialogue and lyrical song in choral parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the appropriateness and distribution of linguistic and musical elements: e.g., whether the choral lyric parts and the dialogic verse each fulfill their distinct roles. Misuse consists in conflating or misplacing the embellishments (e.g., using choral song where dialogue should carry the action).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic emotions: pity (ἔλεος) and fear (φόβος) as the proper affects
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic spectacle must excite the emotions of pity and fear — these are the specific emotions with which tragedy is concerned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the work elicits pity (for an undeserving sufferer) and fear (a self-related apprehension) and whether those emotions are integrated into the dramatic action. The combined effect is crucial; pity alone is not sufficient for full tragic effect (criticisms of views that reduce tragedy to pity only are noted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Katharsis — effecting the proper purgation/purgation of these emotions
rubrics_metrics.description: The function (ὄργον) of tragedy is to effect katharsis (purgation/purification) of the emotions of pity and fear — variously interpreted (medical/purificatory/ethical), but centrally an aesthetic and therapeutic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider katharsis as (a) a pleasurable relief/homoeopathic discharge of overcharged feeling (medical metaphor), (b) purification/clarification of the emotions by expelling morbid elements, and (c) an aesthetic transformation giving refined pleasure. Judge whether the play provides such emotional clarification or merely stimulates undischarged sentiment. Note textual gap: Aristotle's exact account is debated; allow for multiple, related senses (medical, religious, moral).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral end vs. aesthetic end — art must primarily produce refined pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle maintains the end of poetry is a refined pleasure; while poetry may have moral teaching, instructive purpose is secondary — if the poet fails to produce the proper pleasure, he fails as an artist even if morally instructive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating, prioritise artistic/aesthetic efficacy (does the work give the proper pleasure?) over didactic moralizing. A work that teaches well but fails to delight (aesthetic failure) should be judged deficient as poetry. This warns against conflating ethical merit with artistic success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character moral nobility (not mere outward rank)
rubrics_metrics.description: Actors in tragedy ought to be illustrious by moral nobility — the hero should possess moral elevation and dignity; Aristotle demands moral nobility, not simply aristocratic birth or outward rank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the anti-pattern of treating 'nobility' as merely social status; evaluate characters for moral stature, capacity for significant action, and the dignity that makes their fall meaningful. The French critical error (equating σπουδαῖος with high rank) is given as cautionary example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity/identification (ὅμοιος) — the hero must be like us morally
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic sufferer must be 'a man like ourselves' (ὅμοιος): the resemblance in moral character enables sympathy and identification, which are necessary to excite pity and fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the protagonist is recognisably human (shares traits with ordinary human beings) so that audiences can identify and feel the emotional responses. The hero should be elevated yet fundamentally similar enough to provoke self-related fear and pity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heroic mixture: not flawless nor utterly villainous
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic hero should not be of flawless perfection nor of consummate villainy; rather he should be elevated and dignified but possess frailties or errors that make his fall possible and moving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate character complexity: the hero should have a rich humanity — virtues blended with weaknesses — so the downfall appears plausible and elicits pity and fear. Avoid extremes of moral perfection or caricatured villainy; both undermine tragic empathy and katharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of distance/elevation to universalise feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Placing the hero at an ideal distance (raised in dignity or station) provides an impression of grandeur and removes immediate petty self-interests, helping the emotions be refined and universalised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge staging and presentation choices that create an 'ideal distance' (e.g., elevated rank, mythic setting) as tools to refine the audience's emotions and universalise the tragic lessons. Beware making protagonists too like the audience in outward circumstances, which can drag the focus into mundane material concerns rather than universal significance.
